segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Now, a man who took a leap into the unknown, back in 1947. He was a New York City bus driver named William Cimillo. For a while, he became the most famous bus driver in the country. Though, I think what that really means is that he was the only famous bus driver in the country. He told his story on television.

segments.speaker: Announcer
segments.text: Pepsi-Cola presents Faye Emerson.

segments.speaker: Faye Emerson
segments.text: Hello again. Do you ever think of getting away from it all? A bus driver had that same feeling. And he made every headline in the country. So I asked him to come up here and tell us all about it. Hello, Bill.

segments.speaker: William Cimillo
segments.text: Pleasure to meet you.

segments.speaker: Faye Emerson
segments.text: Thank you. Come on. Sit down, and let's talk. Hey, Charlie, you got a couple of Pepsis here for us?

segments.speaker: Charlie
segments.text: Pepsis right here.

segments.speaker: Faye Emerson
segments.text: Thanks, Charlie.

segments.speaker: Charlie
segments.text: Yes, ma'am.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK. So I just want to describe what's happening here. It's black and white. The set of this TV show is a living room, but like a complete living room with everything. Window blinds, paintings on the walls, there's a credenza.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This was back before TV figured out that the only part of the living room that they actually need for a talk show is the couch. So OK. A butler-- yes, a butler-- hands the host, Faye Emerson, a silver tray with a bottle of Pepsi and two glasses. Faye pours her guest a soda and--

segments.speaker: Faye Emerson
segments.text: Will you tell us what happened, please?

segments.speaker: William Cimillo
segments.text: I don't [INAUDIBLE].

segments.speaker: William Cimillo
segments.text: [GLASSES CLINKING]

segments.speaker: Faye Emerson
segments.text: Wonderful.

segments.speaker: William Cimillo
segments.text: Well, it's one of those things. I was on the job for about 20 years, and I really got tired of it all, you know. Up and down, every day, the same people, the same stops, nickels, dimes, transfers, and-- well, this morning, I thought I'd try something different. So I come out of my garage. Instead of making a right turn to go off to my route, I thought I'd make a left turn.

segments.speaker: Faye Emerson
segments.text: And that was the first thought you'd really given to it. Just, you did it on impulse.

segments.speaker: William Cimillo
segments.text: That's right. So I made this left turn, and I went west towards George Washington Bridge. It was a beautiful morning. The sun was shining. So I got on the other side of the Washington Bridge-- I was in Jersey then-- and I stopped for breakfast.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: After breakfast, Cimillo got back in his bus, and he didn't drive to the Bronx to pick up his passengers on his usual route. He headed south on US Route 1. Cimillo had been a bus driver with what was then called the Surface Transportation System of New York for 17 years, without any problems.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Went to work every day, never complained, people said. As he drove further and further away from New York City, and from his job, and from his, you know, life, he switched the destination sign from Subway to Special. Hours passed.

segments.speaker: William Cimillo
segments.text: I kept riding. Before I knew it, I was in Washington. And I was right in front of the White House.

segments.speaker: Faye Emerson
segments.text: You ever been to Washington before?

segments.speaker: William Cimillo
segments.text: Never been there. Never. So I decided to look around. I looked around for 15, 20 minutes. When I come back, there's a policeman standing by the bus. And he asked me, he says, what are you doing here with this great big bus in a restricted parking area?

segments.speaker: Faye Emerson
segments.text: Right in front of the White House, wasn't it?

segments.speaker: William Cimillo
segments.text: Right in front of the place. I said, I'm waiting for a delegation of union officials. They're up there on business. And--

segments.speaker: Faye Emerson
segments.text: Pretty fast thinking.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Cimillo got back in his bus, kept driving south. He said he even picked up a hitchhiker, a sailor, who rode with him for two days.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Then, on the third day, Cimillo and his bus arrived in Hollywood, Florida, just north of Miami. It was late. He said he went for a swim.

segments.speaker: William Cimillo
segments.text: --moonlight bathing. I enjoyed that very much.

segments.speaker: Faye Emerson
segments.text: Oh, what a thrill.

segments.speaker: William Cimillo
segments.text: It was.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: William Cimillo was 1,300 miles from the Bronx. 1,300 miles from New York traffic, from the daily grind. And he was almost out of money. He went to the Gulfstream Park Race Track. He liked to gamble.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We do not know how much money he put down, but he left the track with $2.60. Same day, he also went to the closest Western Union and sent this telegram to his boss. Quote, "With disabled bus number 1310, stop. In need of $50, stop. Send money to Hollywood, Florida, stop. Cimillo."

segments.speaker: William Cimillo
segments.text: So I'm waiting at the telegraph office for the money, and two policemen come over. They says, you're wanted. I said, what for? They says, for stealing a bus. I said, oh no. I didn't steal that bus. I said, they gave it to me. Well, one word led to the other. They said, you're still arrested.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well, today on our radio program, what happens when you take a crazy leap into the unknown, having no idea if it's going to work out, or what's going to happen next. Will you end up on a beach in Florida, happy and carefree? Will you end up in handcuffs? We have three stories of people risking everything in their lives, including the surprising thing that happened next to this bus driver, William Cimillo. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Faye Emerson
segments.text: You did what everybody always wanted to do.

segments.speaker: William Cimillo
segments.text: Just get away from everything. That's what I wanted to do.

segments.speaker: Faye Emerson
segments.text: Talking about getting away from it all. Well, if you are planning to get away from it all, you may like to know that no matter where you go, you're almost sure to find friendly, sparkling, Pepsi-Cola waiting for you.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And of course, feel free to pop open a delicious Pepsi as you listen to this next act, Act One. By the way, we are not getting paid for that at all. Act One, Busman's Holiday.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK. So you remember where we left off. Cimillo had just been arrested in Hollywood, Florida, by two police officers. Joe Richman is the one who dug up this old TV interview, and he picks up the story from there.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: After the arrest, two New York detectives and a mechanic were sent down to Florida to bring Cimillo back, along with his bus. The mechanic drove the bus, but Cimillo told people later, the mechanic couldn't really handle it. His driving made the detectives nervous.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: So the cops actually put Cimillo back behind the wheel. And then right before they arrived in York City, they switched drivers again. They put the mechanic back at the wheel of the bus, and Cimillo dutifully got into his handcuffs.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: So here's what happened next. As the bus pulled up to the steps of the Beach Street Police Station in Manhattan, hundreds of people had gathered, and they were cheering.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: In photographs, you see Cimillo being led through the crowd by the cops, and he has a huge smile. He's beaming. Over the time it took to drive back from Florida to New York, news had spread about the busnapping. William Cimillo had become a folk hero.

segments.speaker: Newscaster
segments.text: William Cimillo. The busman who took a holiday. And brother, what a holiday. Just wanted to drive, feel the tang of spring in the air. Busmen in the Bronx greeted their passengers today with a cry, all aboard for Florida! Ah, spring. But now, here is Don Elda.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: That was NBC. The Daily News wrote, "It must've been a wonderful trip, and we hope Bill's boss will try to understand." From the New York World-Telegram , "We know just how he felt. Who hasn't yearned for escape, for change, for fairer scenes?"

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: From as far away as Michigan, The Traverse City Eagle wrote, "Across the nation today, thousands of office workers and laborers went to their humdrum jobs with hearts a little lighter, because of what William L. Cimillo did to escape the same kind of boredom that fills their ordered lives." Cimillo was indicted on charges of grand larceny. He was facing up to 10 years in prison.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: Cimillo's fellow New York City bus drivers-- who you'd think would be the least sympathetic people in the country to his whole joyride-- they organized a fundraiser to pay his legal fees. Letters and telegrams of support came in from around the country. The court of public opinion was delivering its verdict, and soon, the Surface Transportation System of New York decided to drop the charges.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: Not only that, they gave him his job back. On his first day back on the route, a line of people waited to ride Cimillo's bus. One article reported that after school let out, 350 screaming high school girls tried to get onto his 44-seat bus, ignoring three other buses. They wanted his autograph.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: In the end, William Cimillo was incredibly lucky. He took a huge leap, fled home, cut out on his job, committed a crime, and he got away with it, because people loved the story. For the rest of his life, he was that guy who took a city bus to Florida.

segments.speaker: Richard Cimillo
segments.text: He had his day in the sun.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: This is Richard Cimillo, the bus driver's son. His dad died in 1975.

segments.speaker: Richard Cimillo
segments.text: He just felt like a star, I guess. He was recognized wherever he went. He wasn't just another the bus driver, you know? He was somebody. I guess that's what he felt.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: You say it so begrudgingly, about him being a star. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Richard Cimillo
segments.text: Because, you know, every time we went out, every place we went, there was always-- you know, it was like a movie star. Let me put it to you that way. And after a while, I think my mother got tired of it. And I got tired of it. You know what I'm saying? But he never got tired of it.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: Richard and his family never found the story as charming as most New Yorkers did, starting with the day their dad stole bus number 1310.

segments.speaker: Richard Cimillo
segments.text: Let me explain something to you. I was 12 years old at the time. And after I come home from school, my mother was crying.

segments.speaker: Richard Cimillo
segments.text: And I was, well, Ma, why are you crying? And she said, well, he didn't come home. I wonder where he is. Why wouldn't he come home for supper, and all that. And next day, the same thing. He didn't come home. Not a phone call.

segments.speaker: Richard Cimillo
segments.text: So she called the garage. They didn't know where he is. The bus never come back to the garage. It just disappeared. And so we used to gather together at my grandmother's house. My mother crying, my grandmother crying, it was like a wake.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: I mean, you're 12 years old at the time. What did you think might have happened?

segments.speaker: Richard Cimillo
segments.text: Either the bus ran off the road someplace, maybe went into a lake. This is me thinking, you know. Maybe it was a big accident that nobody knew about. So I really thought, deep down, that he must have died.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: It wasn't until his dad was arrested in Hollywood, Florida, that the family finally knew what had happened. Richard says he never sat down with his dad and really talked about why he did what he did, even as an adult.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: Was it true his dad just got the idea one morning to spontaneously drive to Florida, like he'd said? He didn't plan that at all? Did he really think he'd get away with it? And the biggest question--

segments.speaker: Richard Cimillo
segments.text: I don't know if my mother ever asked, why didn't you call. I never asked. He never called. Not a word. You know, I looked up to him, he was my father.

segments.speaker: Richard Cimillo
segments.text: But after the Florida incident, I had problems. I had problems looking up. That was a tough time for me.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: Even now, the word he uses when he talks about his dad's bus trip is "embarrassing." But there's someone else in the family who has a completely different take on this. Richard's younger brother, Dennis. Quick heads up, their voices are remarkably similar.

segments.speaker: Dennis Cimillo
segments.text: It's a good thing to me. To me, he's still my hero, you know?

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: There's one simple reason the two brothers see this so differently. Dennis was just a baby when their father disappeared. He doesn't remember any of it.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: He doesn't remember his mother and grandmother crying. He didn't think his dad had driven into a lake. He didn't picture him dead in an accident. Dennis' vision of the whole thing is closer to Easy Rider, if Easy Rider took place on a municipal bus.

segments.speaker: Dennis Cimillo
segments.text: I could just see my father [CLAP] putting the pedal to the metal and just go and keep on going. In the drive, just looking out the window and driving. The way my father was, being carefree and saying, you know what? I'm just driving.

segments.speaker: Dennis Cimillo
segments.text: I have nothing on my head. I have no pressure today. I have nothing going on. Let me keep on going.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: Dennis has a collection of memorabilia about the bus trip. He pulls out a large manila folder. On the front it says, Dad's Event. There are dozens of old photographs and articles, and a videotape with footage from 1947. We go down to the basement to watch it.

segments.speaker: Dennis Cimillo
segments.text: This is from an old newsreel that was taken at the time. It's really short. That's the bus coming in.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: It's his dad, arriving back in New York.

segments.speaker: Dennis Cimillo
segments.text: And right now he's being escorted into the courthouse, going in front of the judge, and being arraigned right now. That's it.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: Now, Richard, the older brother, he had told me about the same newsreel. He had seen it the week it was actual news, in a movie theater, when he was 12.

segments.speaker: Richard Cimillo
segments.text: I'm sitting there, and all of a sudden, boom. My father's picture is up on the screen. And I'm looking there, I was stunned. You see your father, as a kid, handcuffed, detectives on both sides of him, bringing him into the courthouse. I don't know anybody that would feel proud of something like that.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: So that's the older brother, Richard. But here in the basement with Dennis, his take on this--

segments.speaker: Dennis Cimillo
segments.text: I enjoy every minute of it. Just makes me idolize him. I wish I could do things like that sometimes.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: In a way, a small way, Dennis has done that. He sees himself as a free spirit. He says he got that from his dad. He doesn't worry about things too much.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: He likes to gamble. He started his own businesses distributing beer and soda. He was his own boss, which meant no pension, no paid vacation, no security, no guarantees. He says it's different from the life his brother chose.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: And Richard, the older brother, would agree with that. The lesson Richard took from his father's story was to be a responsible person, to think about the consequences of his actions.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: Richard worked all his life as a fireman, which oddly, he calls a safe job. He's retired now. But as it turned out, when I interviewed Richard, he and his wife were getting ready to drive to Florida, as he said, the legit way.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: Did you ever want to do something like what your dad did? Did you ever want to--

segments.speaker: Richard Cimillo
segments.text: No, no, no. No. No. I knew I didn't want to do something as drastic as that. So that's the biggest difference between my father and me. My father never worried.

segments.speaker: Richard Cimillo
segments.text: Don't worry, the rent will be paid. Don't worry, we've got this food on the table. Don't worry about it. I worry about everything. I worry about my kids. They had to go to school. They had to go to college.

segments.speaker: Richard Cimillo
segments.text: I worry about the snow. [LAUGHS] My father never worried about nothing. My father never worried about nothing. He worried-- you know, I worry. I don't sleep nights. I toss and turn, I'm still worrying. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: So you wish you didn't worry as much?

segments.speaker: Richard Cimillo
segments.text: I wish I could've lived that-- yeah. I wish I could not worry.

segments.speaker: Joe Richman
segments.text: After Richard's dad, William Cimillo, got his job back in 1947, he went on to drive a bus in the Bronx for the next 16 years, with no detours. Once, a reporter asked him, do you still think about hitting the open road? Turning left and heading across the bridge again? Cimillo said, yes, he thought about it. But when you tell somebody a joke, he said, it's never as funny the second time.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Joe Richmond. Sarah Kate Kramer produced that story with him. That's part of their podcast series, Radio Diaries, which you can find and subscribe to at radiodiaries.org.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Two, Where We're Going, We Don't Need Roads. So now a story about people who want to take a different kind of leap, a kind of quantum leap, you could say.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There was this study done by the Pew Research Center and Smithsonian Magazine back in February, published in April. The study was about future technologies. And basically, they called up 1,001 Americans.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I do not understand why it's 1,001 and not just 1,000. Maybe 1,001 just seemed sexier or something. Anyway, they called up 1,001 people. They asked them what new technological advances they expected to see in the future, and what technological advances they wanted to see.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So there were questions like, would you eat meat that was grown in a lab? Would you get a brain implant to improve your mental capacity? The answer is yes and yes to those, of course. And if you read through the whole thing, there's this kind of bizarre finding at the end, something small, something that caught the interest of producers Sean Cole and Jonathan Goldstein.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: So the very last question in the survey about future technologies, question 14-- it was a short survey-- was this. If there was one futuristic invention that you could own, what would it be? There was no multiple choice. This was an open-ended question. And off the tops of their heads, 9% of respondents, so roughly 1 out of 10 people, said they wanted some way to travel through time.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: One out of 10 came up with that on their own. That'd be roughly 30 million Americans. That's like the entire nation of Canada sitting around, wishing for a time machine. Which, speaking as a Canadian, I can say we secretly do. First stop, moments before making our national mascot a beaver and not an American woodcock.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: The desire for time travel, at 9%, ranked highest on the list, tied only with cures for diseases.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: People wanted time travel more than they wanted robot servants, which was 4%.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: More than they wanted world peace, a whopping 2%.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Time travel was three times more popular than hover cars, holodecks, and jet packs combined.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: But the Pew study is just a study. It's just numbers. It doesn't explain why so many people want to travel in time. Is it our curiosity about the future?

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: I wonder what new kinds of cutlets the world of tomorrow will hold?

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Regrets over the past?

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Boy, do I wish I hadn't eaten all those cutlets.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: And so we struck out into the world to try to answer that question. Why do you want to time travel?

segments.speaker: Man 1
segments.text: This is something I think about a lot.

segments.speaker: Man 2
segments.text: Oh, well, I've done a lot of thinking about this.

segments.speaker: Man 3
segments.text: Oh, there's a lot of things I'd like to accomplish.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: And even though they've been mulling this over for so long, many still reach for the most well-trodden sci-fi comic book staple.

segments.speaker: Man 4
segments.text: My first impulse about time travel is the same one that I would guess that everybody has. You know, thinking that I'm going to go back and I'm going to kill Hitler.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: What's funny is that they know it's kind of lame. You can hear it in their voices.

segments.speaker: Man 4
segments.text: Or kill Hitler when he's a baby, or kill his mother or something.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: They preface it with phrases like--

segments.speaker: Woman 1
segments.text: It's the thing everyone always says is--

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: And then they say it anyway.

segments.speaker: Woman 1
segments.text: If there hadn't been a Hitler--

segments.speaker: Man 5
segments.text: Put a bullet in Adolf Hitler's head when he was still a student, I guess.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: We spoke to about 50 people, both friends and strangers we walked up to on the street.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Most of them had more thoughts about traveling to the past, rather than the future. After all, you never know with the future. Teleport yourself hundreds of years from now, and you could land on an Earth devoid of people, where the only remaining structure is a monument to President Donald Trump, made out of eternium.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Whereas with the past, at least you know the basic plot points. And there's a vast encyclopedia of calamities you could still fix.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: If you could go back in time and do anything you want, what would it be?

segments.speaker: Man On Street 1
segments.text: I have no idea. Warn people of disasters, I guess?

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Warn people of disasters?

segments.speaker: Man On Street 1
segments.text: Yeah. Like, September 11, or something.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: And how would you go about it, do you think?

segments.speaker: Man On Street 1
segments.text: Oh, I have no idea. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: And of course, no one imagines that they'll end up with an iron collar around their neck, working in a quarry. Instead, they have a starring role in the historical docu-drama. Like this guy, who'd set the controls for the Revolutionary War.

segments.speaker: Man On Street 2
segments.text: I don't think I'd be like, a general in the field or anything like that. But I'd probably be more of like an adviser to Washington. Like Alexander Hamilton was, right? And a few other folks. So yeah.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: I love how you're already an officer in this.

segments.speaker: Man On Street 2
segments.text: Exactly. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: But these ambitious, world-saving time travelers are just a small subset of the people we interviewed.

segments.speaker: Woman On Street 1
segments.text: I have a probably much more selfish kind of answer. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Most of the people we talked to didn't want to change history. They wanted to go back in time to fix something personal, something in their own lives.

segments.speaker: Man On Street 3
segments.text: Probably wouldn't have asked my ex-wife out that first time.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Really?

segments.speaker: Man On Street 3
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: And how do you think you would be different now in that case?

segments.speaker: Man On Street 3
segments.text: I'd have a hell of a lot more money.

segments.speaker: Man On Street 4
segments.text: There were some people that I wish I could have punched. One of them is deceased.

segments.speaker: Girl
segments.text: If I could time travel, I'd go back and fix all the awful, awful mistakes I'd done. Because there's so many stuff that you just think of, like when you're lying in bed, you're like, oh my God, that's so embarrassing.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Well, wait. Hang on a second though. You're only 11.

segments.speaker: Girl
segments.text: Yeah. I've got a lot of things I want to change.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: She told me, number one on the list, the night she told a room full of adults a joke that began, a Canadian, an Italian and two Chinese people were standing on a roof.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: More than one person said they wanted to go back in time just to advise their younger selves, knowing what they know now. Like my friend Jimmy.

segments.speaker: Jimmy
segments.text: I think I would meet myself at whatever coffee shop I used to go to. It was like the Derne Street Deli on the back end of Beacon Hill. I'd be like, look, kid, come here for a minute. Come here. These are the five things you need to know that's going to help you in the next 25 years of your life. These are the five things you need to know.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: And what are those five things?

segments.speaker: Jimmy
segments.text: Bet on these sports games. Never ride this roller coaster. And sex moves.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Two other things?

segments.speaker: Jimmy
segments.text: Oh, the sex moves was three things.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: And listening to both of these groups, the ones who want to save the world, and the ones who'd use the time machine to excel in the boudoir--

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Or to do anything else in their private life.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: --you can't help wondering, are the people who want to save the world just better people? We posed this question to everyone we talked to.

segments.speaker: Man On Street 5
segments.text: I mean, do I think they're better people? I think it's just-- those people are less self-involved. That doesn't make them better or worse.

segments.speaker: Jimmy
segments.text: I don't know. I think that that sort of grand delusion that you could ultimately change a big event, a big life-changing event, and that you'd be doing everybody a favor by doing this, is a little-- I mean, that's pretty crazy. As opposed to thinking, oh yeah. I could make myself not ride the J train that night when that dude threw up on me.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: When you talk to a large number of people about time travel, you tend to hear a lot about the butterfly effect. That idea that a little change can have massive repercussions as it echoes through history. You've heard of this. But with these small, little personal wishes, it almost feels like you can get away with it somehow. It's just you, after all, and maybe one other person.

segments.speaker: Woman On Street 2

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Sounds like a stand up guy.

segments.speaker: Tina Dupuy
segments.text: Yeah, right? He's like, it's OK. And he's like, you don't have to do it. You don't have to drink. Or if you want to, great.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: I mean, I feel like one of the indicators of not being an alcoholic is having a casual take-it-or-leave-it relationship.

segments.speaker: Tina Dupuy
segments.text: Thank you. See? That's why I was an alcoholic. [LAUGHS] Because it was the mental obsession.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Right, right. So the fact that you're obsessively talking about, shouldn't I, should I, should I, I mean, did that-- is that the reason that you were having the conversation over and over again? Because every time you had that conversation, that would reinforce the idea that you were an alcoholic, because here you are, bringing it up again. And if you were not an alcoholic, you wouldn't need to be having this conversation as many times as you were.

segments.speaker: Tina Dupuy
segments.text: Absolutely.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Wow.

segments.speaker: Tina Dupuy
segments.text: Right. So and then the only way to get out of that is to really like, let's do this. We go to a wine store on the way home. We pay for it.

segments.speaker: Tina Dupuy
segments.text: We go home. My husband makes a pasta dish with chicken. He lights two candles, pours two glasses of wine. And so I take a little sip--

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: And?

segments.speaker: Tina Dupuy
segments.text: --and I say, it tastes like the '70s.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: [LAUGHS] Meaning?

segments.speaker: Tina Dupuy
segments.text: Meaning I had tasted white wine before, but I was like five. I was young. But I remember that taste. That taste immediately came back to me. And then I tried to eat my meal, and it was-- I didn't enjoy the taste. It was really acidic.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: And were you waiting to--

segments.speaker: Tina Dupuy
segments.text: Oh yeah. So I was like, when am I going to want to like, go and do shots at the corner bar? I mean, who knows? And I went to sleep. You know. Had a glass of wine, and it was completely uneventful.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: I just want to make sure I'm understanding. You are saying you don't think you're an alcoholic.

segments.speaker: Tina Dupuy
segments.text: I'm not an alcoholic. Not by any measure.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: And now you drink--

segments.speaker: Tina Dupuy
segments.text: Now I drink. I'm new at this, right? So I've been drinking for about seven months now. And if I drink more than two, I go to sleep.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: It hasn't changed anything else in your life.

segments.speaker: Tina Dupuy
segments.text: Not at all. I've had no personality change. I've had none of-- when I start to feel the effects of alcohol, I stop drinking. Now that I actually know what alcoholism is and what normal drinking is-- more importantly, I know what normal drinking is.

segments.speaker: Tina Dupuy
segments.text: I'm average. Which is probably the most jarring thing that has happened, that after all of this, I'm incredibly average when it comes to my alcohol consumption.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Have you told everyone you care about?

segments.speaker: Tina Dupuy
segments.text: I've told a very select group of people that I'm drinking. Because one, I'm afraid that people who I have helped over the years in AA will be affected, and it'll make them question their alcoholism. And maybe if they drink again, then I'll feel responsible.

segments.speaker: Tina Dupuy
segments.text: There's also the aspect of that I was lying. I mean, I was lying. I was lying to myself. But I was lying. And so I am embarrassed. It seems like I just took a long time to fig-- it's like, it's embarrassing that I didn't have this kind of self awareness.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: The postscript to drinking for Tina has been getting straight in her mind why she thought she was an alcoholic in the first place. How does a non-alcoholic child come to believe that she's a stone drunk? Well, here's how she puts it together now.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: She went to the first AA meeting just because, nothing else to do. This was in the place she was being held before going to the group home at 13. And one of the AA phrases that caught Tina's ear was, relate to the feelings. Because boy, did she relate.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: In AA, she heard other people talk, one after another, about things that were so familiar to her. Feeling rejected by their families, winding up in hospital or rehab, feeling trapped and furious and desperate. People said to her, I used to be exactly where you are now. And they had all done what she had done. They had lashed out. They had acted badly.

segments.speaker: Tina Dupuy
segments.text: There was no other way of explaining at the time. And it wasn't until, I mean, this is very recently, there was no way for me to figure out why I kept on getting locked up. Why I kept on being sent away. Why my mother was fuming at me.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: If Tina was an alcoholic, everything made sense. She was the problem. She was the only problem, and if she stuck with the program, she could fix the problem.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: AA gave Tina a whole life-- goals, discipline, a belief system, people to call when things were bad, people to call when things were good. She graduated from high school at 17, emancipated herself from foster care, started her adult life.

segments.speaker: Tina Dupuy
segments.text: It's really liberating to find your people. To find people who you relate to. To find people that ask you to come back. And that was what I experienced. I didn't have people asking me to come back.

segments.speaker: Tina Dupuy
segments.text: And they said at every meeting, keep coming back. And I was like, OK. I became a contributing member of society. I mean, that's a phrase that they use. But I stopped feeling sorry for myself.

segments.speaker: Tina Dupuy
segments.text: I looked at other people whose lives were much more difficult, for whatever reason, and I stopped feeling sorry for the lot I was given. And being able to feel true happiness, just feeling like I was OK, and there was no crisis, that was what I learned in Alcoholics Anonymous. That is the irony, right? I'm not an alcoholic, but my life was saved by AA.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: I asked Tina if any of her friends are worried about her now that she's drinking. She said, no, not anymore. But she said, sometimes she still has a little voice in her head, saying, yeah you're fine now.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: But what if there's some threshold you just haven't crossed, and when you do, you turn into the full-blown drunk you always thought you were? But the voice has zero evidence for that scenario. It's just trying to keep the story going.

segments.speaker: Tina Dupuy
